qs.q: A 62-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease develops cor pulmonale with right ventricular hypertrophy. Which of the following mechanisms best explains the adaptive change in the right ventricle?
qs.e: Cardiac myocytes are permanent cells that cannot divide. Hypertrophy results from increased workload (pressure overload from pulmonary hypertension) causing increased synthesis of myofilaments and enlargement of existing cells, not an increase in cell number.

qs.q: In which CHD does the right ventricle inflow tract function haemodynamically as an atrial chamber?
o: Septum secundum → ostium primum → ostium secundum → fossa ovalis
Ostium primum → ostium secundum → septum secundum → fossa ovalis
Septum primum → ostium primum → ostium secundum → septum secundum
Fossa ovalis → septum primum → ostium primum → septum secundum
qs.e: Apical displacement of the septal tricuspid leaflet causes atrialization of the RV inflow tract — it receives atrial pressure and contracts out of synchrony with the functional RV.

qs.q: Which congenital heart defect is characterised by absence of a direct connection between the right atrium and right ventricle?
qs.e: There is no tricuspid valve orifice connecting RA to RV. Survival depends on an ASD for right-sided drainage and a VSD or PDA for pulmonary blood flow.

faq.a: The RV wall is thin and cannot generate high pressures; chronic pressure overload leads to hypertrophy then dilatation and failure.

exam: A 45‑year‑old man with HIV presents with peripheral edema, JVD and a parasternal heave – what is your next bedside investigation and why? — Assess for RV overload with ECG and, if possible, bedside echocardiography; clinical signs guide urgency when imaging is unavailable.

Explain how chronic schistosomiasis can lead to right‑ventricular failure. — Schistosoma haematobium causes portal hypertension, leading to pulmonary hypertension via embolic emboli; sustained afterload overload hypertrophies the RV.

A patient with rheumatic mitral stenosis develops sudden dyspnoea and clear lungs; what distinguishes RV failure from left‑sided decompensation? — Look for JVD, hepatomegaly, and a loud P2; absence of pulmonary crackles points to isolated RV strain.

Why is intravenous nitroprusside avoided in acute RV failure? — It reduces systemic vascular resistance, potentially worsening hypotension without lowering pulmonary pressures; selective pulmonary vasodilators are preferred.

In a low‑resource hospital without echo, how would you estimate pulmonary artery pressure? — Use clinical signs (loud P2, RV heave, Kussmaul’s sign) and chest X‑ray for pulmonary artery enlargement; combine into a bedside RV failure score.

A child with sickle cell disease presents with acute chest syndrome and right‑sided heart strain; what immediate management steps protect the RV? — Provide oxygen, treat pain, give simple transfusion, and avoid fluid overload; monitor for pulmonary hypertension.

Differentiate between massive pulmonary embolism and acute RV infarction on bedside exam. — PE shows sudden dyspnoea, pleuritic pain, and often a new right‑sided heart sound; RV infarction follows inferior MI, with hypotension, clear lungs, and ST elevation in II, III, aVF.

What is the significance of a reduced TAPSE on echo for RV function? — TAPSE <16 mm indicates impaired RV systolic motion and predicts poorer prognosis; if echo unavailable, rely on clinical RV failure score.
ai.title: Right Ventricle
ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: The right ventricle receives systemic venous blood and pumps it to the pulmonary circulation. Its thin wall and unique geometry make it vulnerable to pressure overload and volume overload, especially in low‑resource settings.

b: Thin muscular wall (≈3‑5 mm) compared with left ventricle
High compliance – accommodates large volume changes
Normal systolic pressure ≈25 mmHg, diastolic pressure ≈5 mmHg
sections.p: The right ventricle (RV) sits anteriorly, wraps around the left ventricle, and has a crescent shape. It receives blood from the right atrium through the tricuspid valve and ejects it through the pulmonary valve into the pulmonary artery.

b: Preload ↑ → dilatation, may improve stroke volume until wall stress limits output
Afterload ↑ (pulmonary hypertension) → RV hypertrophy then failure
Contractility ↓ (ischemia, myocarditis) → low output despite normal pressures
sections.p: RV performance depends on preload, afterload, and contractility. In low‑resource settings, chronic lung disease, pulmonary embolism, and rheumatic heart disease are common drivers of RV dysfunction.

b: Pulsatile liver, clear lungs unless left‑sided disease coexists
sections.p: RV failure presents with systemic venous congestion, a loud P2, and a parasternal heave. Recognising the pattern guides urgent investigations and therapy, especially when echocardiography is scarce.

t.b: Is there pulmonary artery enlargement or pleural effusion? → Suggests pulmonary hypertension or RV overload; if unavailable, rely on clinical signs.
Are there right‑axis deviation or R‑wave in V1? → Supports RV strain; if ECG not possible, use bedside auscultation.
What is RV size, function, and pulmonary artery pressure? → Confirms RV dilatation, reduced TAPSE, estimate PASP; if absent, use clinical scoring (e.g., RV failure score).

b: Palpable parasternal heave → RV pressure overload
Loud, single S2 with accentuated P2 → pulmonary hypertension
Kussmaul’s sign (rise in JVP on inspiration) → constrictive pericarditis or severe RV dysfunction
sections.p: During bedside assessment, focus on signs that differentiate isolated RV failure from biventricular failure and from left‑sided causes of dyspnoea.

b: Ignoring the absence of pulmonary crackles in isolated RV failure
Assuming all JVD is due to heart failure without checking for tamponade or tension pneumothorax
Relying solely on chest X‑ray when radiographs are poor quality
sections.p: Students often mistake peripheral edema from RV failure for primary renal disease, or attribute a loud P2 to left‑sided valve disease.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden hypotension with clear lungs – possible massive pulmonary embolism
Rapidly rising JVP with pulsus paradoxus – suspect cardiac tamponade
Severe hypoxaemia despite oxygen – acute RV failure from pulmonary hypertension crisis
